2.1 — Coins: Triggers, Tags & Your First Stat

Your character can walk, but it cannot touch anything. Walk straight over the coin and nothing happens — not because your code is wrong, but because nothing in this entire project is built to notice a collision. Today you make the first object in the game that reacts to the player, and in doing so you switch the physics engine on for good.

The Problem ~10 min

Your goal: make a coin disappear when the player touches it. Before you write a single line, answer this honestly — how would Unity ever know the two objects touched? The Player has a Transform. The Coin has a Transform. Two positions in space do not collide. Nothing in the engine is checking.

Something has to tell it what shape each object is, and something has to be simulated every frame so those shapes can be tested against each other. Read what Unity gives you:

ComponentWhat it contributes
Collider2D Gives an object a shape the physics engine can test against other shapes. Without one, an object is invisible to physics — it is only a picture.
Rigidbody2D Puts an object under simulation: the engine tracks it every physics step, and it is what makes overlap messages fire at all.
Is Trigger (checkbox on any Collider2D) Changes what an overlap means. A solid collider pushes objects apart. A trigger does not push — it only reports that the overlap happened.
OnTriggerEnter2D The message your script receives on the first frame two shapes overlap. This is the event a coin pickup is built on.
CompareTag How you check what you just touched. Asks the engine whether a collider carries a given tag.
The rule that catches everyone. Unity's 2D physics only simulates objects that have a Collider2D, and overlap messages only fire when at least one of the two objects also has a Rigidbody2D. Two colliders with no body anywhere produce silence — no error, no warning, nothing to debug.

And here is the part that matters today: in this project nothing in Assets/Prefabs has either one — except the Switch. Not the Player. Not the Coin. Not the Spikes. You are about to be the first person to give anything in this game a physics body.

Socratic: What Is a Collider For?

  1. A Transform stores position, rotation and scale. What does a Collider2D store that a Transform has no way to express?
  2. The physics engine runs on its own schedule, not inside your Update(). Why would Unity be built that way, instead of letting your script test for overlaps once a frame?
  3. A trigger pushes nothing — it only reports. Name two game behaviours besides a coin pickup where a report-only overlap is the right tool.
  4. A collider is a shape; a rigidbody is a thing under simulation. The Player is the object that moves. Which of the two must live on the Player for a coin to ever notice it, and which one could live on the coin instead?
  5. The minimum is "a collider on both, a body on one". Which object should carry the body — the coin that sits still and vanishes, or the player that moves all game? Argue it, then build it that way.
Read Function-Level Examples ~15 min

Read each snippet for what it does in isolation, then work out how it maps onto your coin. None of these is from a video game.

Example 1 — Receiving overlap events on an automatic grocery store door:

private void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D entrant)
{
    Debug.Log("Motion sensor tripped by: " + entrant.name);
}

Example 2 — Validating identity with tags on a vault keycard scanner:

if (incomingItem.CompareTag("SecurityKeycard"))
{
    Debug.Log("Access granted.");
}

Example 3 — Memory cleanup on a spent rocket stage:

Destroy(spentBoosterStage.gameObject);

Example 4 — An airport baggage carousel (comment only):

// The scanner arch is a trigger. Luggage only trips it while it is riding
// the belt - a bag the belt never moves is invisible to the arch.

Example 5 — An overhead air-hockey table (comment only):

// Seen from directly above, a puck has no "down" to fall toward.
// The table is the whole world, so gravity is switched off.

Predict Before Building

  1. In the door snippet, entrant is a Collider2D, not a GameObject. How do you get from it to the object's name and its tag?
  2. In the rocket snippet, what would Destroy(spentBoosterStage) actually destroy if the variable were typed as a Collider2D? What does .gameObject add?
  3. The bags on the carousel only trip the arch while the belt is moving them. What is the minimum this project needs for a coin to notice the player — a body on the coin, a body on the player, or both?
  4. The air-hockey puck has gravity switched off. Predict what your top-down player will do if you add a Rigidbody2D and leave Gravity Scale at its default of 1. Write the prediction down before you test it in the Build Lab.
  5. A coin that stopped you dead like a wall would be terrible. Which checkbox makes that difference, and what is the name of the message you receive instead?
  6. When you walk into a coin, whose collider arrives in the other parameter — yours or the coin's? How could you prove it with a Debug.Log?
Build Lab: Give the Player a Body ~25 min

Step 1 — get a coin within reach. The Overworld scene ships with exactly one Coin instance. Find it, or drag a couple more from Assets/Prefabs and spread them out. Put one somewhere you will walk.

Step 2 — the discovery. Select the Assets/Prefabs/Coin asset and read its Inspector. Now select the Player and read its Inspector. List every component each one has — and then write down what is missing from both.

Architectural specification: the Coin.
  • Which component gives an object a shape the physics engine can test? Where do you add it in the Inspector?
  • Should a coin be a solid collider or an Is Trigger zone? Describe what the game would feel like if a coin stopped you in your tracks like a wall.
  • A default collider is sized from the sprite's import bounds — and remember from 1.2 that the Coin's Sprite Renderer is on a child object. Does the collider you just added actually cover the coin you can see? How would you check?
  • The coin's tag is already Coin on the prefab. Does a tag live on the prefab asset or on the instance in the scene? Change an instance's tag and find out which one wins.
Architectural specification: the Player.
  • Which component makes an object visible to the physics engine — the one without which OnTriggerEnter2D never fires at all?
  • Where should the Player's collider go — on the root, or on the child Sprite that owns the renderer? What problem appears if you put a default-sized collider on the root? Press Play and find out.
  • A top-down world has no "down". What should Gravity Scale be — and what does your character do if you leave it at 1? Compare that against the prediction you wrote down a moment ago.
  • A dynamic body that clips something will also spin. Which Rigidbody2D setting stops your character tumbling when it grazes a wall?
Architectural specification: the code.
  • Which method receives the overlap message on the Player, and what is the parameter's type? When you walk into a coin, which object does that parameter represent?
  • How do you check that the thing you touched is a coin? Why is CompareTag better than comparing tag strings with ==?
  • You want the coin to vanish, not the player. Is it gameObject or other.gameObject — and what happens if you get it backwards?
  • How many coins you have collected is a fact about the player. Where does that field live? Write it, and print the new total with Debug.Log so a player can watch the number change with no UI at all.
A body changes the whole game — go and see what you broke. The moment the Player has a Collider2D and a Rigidbody2D, every collider in the scene starts interacting with it. That includes the Cave Entrances, which carry solid colliders wired to a scene-switching script that has been sitting dormant this whole time, precisely because your Player had no collider to trip it.

So: walk into a cave mouth and find out what happens. If you are suddenly standing in a different scene, nothing is broken — you switched the physics engine on. Write down what happened and why. Do not fix it yet, and do not delete the cave entrances: Unit 5 builds the cave properly, and this is the first thread of it.
One number, one home. For now the coin count lives on PlayerController. There is a StatManager.cs in Assets/Scripts — it is empty, and it stays empty. Later in the year you will have a real reason to move your stats into a manager, and that reason will come from a scene change, not from tidiness. Until then, every stat you build belongs to the player.
Read the Docs: Where Should a Stat Live? ~10 min

You just made a real design decision without being told to. Here are the three honest options for where a number like "coins" can live, and what each one costs:

ApproachWhat it looks likeWhat it costsWhen it wins
(a) A field on PlayerController [SerializeField] private int coins; The player owns the number, so anything else that wants it must find the player first. Now. The only thing that touches coins is the player.
(b) A separate PlayerStats component The numbers live in a component whose only job is numbers. One more component, one more reference to cache, one more thing to keep in sync. When PlayerController grows long enough that movement code and stat code start fighting over the same file.
(c) A global singleton StatManager Any script, anywhere, reads the numbers from one shared object. Everything can reach it, so nothing protects it — and to be worth having at all, it must survive a scene change. When several systems need the same numbers and those numbers must outlive a scene load.

Where Does a Number Belong?

  1. Which of the three did you just build, and which line of your own code proves it?
  2. Open Assets/Scripts/StatManager.cs and read it. If you filled it in as a singleton today, would your coin count survive a scene change? Would that be a feature or a problem right now?
  3. The coin disappears when collected, but "how many coins I have" is not a property of the coin. So where does that number really belong — the object that vanishes, or the object that persists?
  4. Which option makes the number easiest to find when you reopen this project in three weeks, and which makes it easiest to test on its own?
  5. You just watched a cave entrance teleport you somewhere. What does that tell you about whether your stats need to survive a scene change this month?
Bug Hunt: Tracing Pickup Bugs ~15 min

Bug Hunt

  1. Untick Is Trigger on the coin's collider. Does OnTriggerEnter2D still run? What happens instead, and where does the player end up?
  2. Remove the Rigidbody2D from the Player but leave every collider in place. Does the coin still vanish? Does the Console show a message, or nothing at all?
  3. Change your destroy call to Destroy(gameObject) and collect a coin. Which object disappeared — and what is the Console still printing that tells you the player survived?
  4. Comment out the destroy line and walk in and out of the same coin five times. What does the count say? Why is a coin that pays out every time a bug rather than a bonus?
  5. Set the Player's Gravity Scale back to 1. What does the character do when you stop pressing keys, and which setting was quietly doing the work all along?
  6. Walk into a Cave Entrance deliberately with your new body and collider. Which two components you added are responsible — and given the tag check inside that script, why did it react to you and not to a wall?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Destroy versus SetActive

  1. Replace Destroy(other.gameObject) with other.gameObject.SetActive(false). What changes on screen, what is different in the Hierarchy after you stop playing, and what happens to your count?
  2. Read the docs for SetActive. In a game with thousands of coins, why might switching an object off and reusing it beat destroying it and building a new one?
  3. Open Assets/Scripts/Package Scripts/SceneSwitch.cs and find the method that fires when the player touches a cave mouth. Which parameter type does it take, and which of the two components you added today made it fire?
  4. Print your coin count with Debug.Log every frame instead of only on pickup. What happens to the Console, and why was printing on the event the better choice?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain what a Collider2D is for, and what a Rigidbody2D adds on top of it
  • State the rule — colliders on both, a body on at least one — and say which object you gave the body to, and why
  • Explain trigger versus solid, and defend the coin's choice
  • Explain what the parameter in OnTriggerEnter2D actually refers to
  • Explain why CompareTag beats comparing tag strings
  • State where the coin count lives, and name one alternative you rejected, with a reason
  • Explain what happened at the cave entrance, and why it is not a bug
  • Commit and push
